source.title: Adversarial Concurrent Training: Optimizing Robustness and Accuracy Trade-off of Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: E. Arani; Fahad Sarfraz; Bahram Zonooz

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports clean accuracy and random-label fitting measurements, but does not test the natural-label train–test generalization claim or any listed version. Its random-label experiment fits labels on frozen representations and measures training accuracy; it does not pair that result with held-out accuracy for the same network trained on natural labels.
record.gate_note: The paper reports clean accuracy for adversarially trained models and a frozen-representation random-label fitting experiment. These results concern the claim's subject but do not measure the behavior named by V1–V8. Figure 3's random-label values are shown in the figure and described in text; the text does not state the exact values.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates ACT's robustness–accuracy trade-off, frozen-representation random-label fitting, weight norms and posterior entropy. None measures a listed version: the random-label probe changes the trainable system, and posterior entropy is not magnitude-aware sharpness or a generalization gap.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: ACT improves the robustness–generalization trade-off, and their analyses suggest lower model complexity, greater representation compression and higher posterior entropy indicative of flatter minima. These are the authors' interpretations; flatness is not directly measured, and ACT F's compression probe improves over normal training but not over Madry or TRADES.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes collaborative adversarial and natural model training, and compares it with Madry and TRADES adversarial training. It does not reproduce the methods in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the ACT balancing factor α affects natural and robust accuracy; Table 1 varies α for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10. It also reports results across datasets and architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: ACT changes clean accuracy relative to adversarial-training baselines, with direction depending on dataset and architecture; on ImageNet it reaches 68.20% versus Madry's 65.70%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concurrent natural and adversarial training can improve the robustness–accuracy trade-off.

fits_no_version.finding: Random-label training accuracy on frozen representations is 68.71% for ACT F and 53.93% for ACT G, versus 75.47% for normal training, 55.71% for Madry and 54.41% for TRADES. ACT G fits less than all comparators; ACT F fits less than normal training but more than Madry and TRADES.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training methods change how readily an added MLP fits random labels using frozen representations.

fits_no_version.finding: ACT has lower layerwise Frobenius norms and higher average training-sample posterior entropy. Neither analysis measures magnitude-aware sharpness or its association with train–test gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ACT changes weight magnitudes and predictive entropy relative to adversarial-training baselines.

record.problems: The random-label fitting comparison concerns an added MLP on frozen representations, not the same network trained end-to-end on random labels; it reports no test accuracy for that experiment. The exact Figure 3 random-label values are not stated in prose. The paper reports mean and one standard deviation over three random seeds for its experiments unless otherwise stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows beyond the reported clean standard accuracies and the two plotted ACT random-label fitting values. Other table metrics concern adversarial robustness or minimum perturbation rather than the claim's generalization subject.

untested.parts: Matched architecture and training recipe fitting random labels nearly perfectly while generalizing on natural labels; held-out random-label accuracy at chance.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under matched epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions, dataset-size dependence and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps and its ranking against other measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equal-sized random removals.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation='tests' conflicts with its otherwise appropriate T6 rationale. Clean accuracy is presented as standard generalization performance; exclusion from the versions rests on missing claim-specific comparisons, not on requiring a train–test gap for every generalization claim. No additional results bearing on V1–V8 were found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether the same network and recipe fit random labels and generalize on held-out natural labels, or whether random-label held-out accuracy stays at chance.
No width sweep or test-error result beyond the interpolation threshold.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks on image generalization.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison for held-out performance.
No batch-size comparison of held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
No dropout intervention or dropout and weight-decay removal comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison with generalization gaps.
No removal of memorized examples or retraining comparison.
